content.title: Designing Follow-Up Experiments
content.overview: Designing a follow-up experiment involves isolating a specific new factor to determine its effect on a previously observed outcome. On the ACT, this requires selecting a single independent variable, maintaining strict controls, and ensuring sufficient sample sizes to produce valid results.
learning_objectives: Identify a single independent variable and its concrete levels for a follow-up study.
Maintain experimental controls by keeping original conditions identical.
Define a specific dependent measurement and timing for data collection.
Apply sampling requirements, including random assignment and minimum sample sizes.

sections.title: Isolating the Independent Variable
sections.content: A valid follow-up experiment must test exactly one new factor, known as the independent variable. This is the condition you deliberately change to see if it affects the outcome. You must define concrete levels for this variable—for example, if testing 'temperature,' the levels might be 20°C and 30°C. Testing more than one new variable at a time creates confounding results, making it impossible to tell which change caused the effect.

sections.title: Maintaining Controls and Constants
sections.content: To ensure the validity of a follow-up, all other conditions from the original experiment must remain identical. These are called controls. If the original study used a specific soil type, light intensity, or duration, the follow-up must use those same parameters. This ensures that any difference in the dependent variable (the outcome being measured) is solely due to the new independent variable.

sections.title: Measurement and Sampling Standards
sections.content:
A robust design requires a clear dependent measurement (e.g., 'mean plant height in cm') and a specific timeframe for measurement (e.g., 'after 14 days'). Furthermore, to ensure statistical reliability, the ACT Science section looks for random assignment of subjects to groups and a sufficient sample size. A general rule for these designs is to use at least 6 samples per level (n ≥ 6) to effectively isolate effects and reduce the impact of outliers.

![A flowchart showing the steps to design a follow-up experiment: Identify 1 Variable, Set Concrete Levels, Maintain Controls, and Define Sampling.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/710b1463-fd25-45af-8e8d-c0d78452d4c8-1786506688241-180.webp)

worked_examples.question: Original study: A scientist found that Bacteria X grows faster in Liquid Media A than in Liquid Media B at 37°C over 24 hours (n=10 per group). Design a follow-up experiment to test whether the presence of UV light changes the growth rate in these media.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Identify the new independent variable. The variable is 'UV light presence' with two levels: 'UV light exposed' and 'No UV light (dark)'. Step 2: Maintain controls. Keep the media types (A and B), the temperature (37°C), and the duration (24 hours) the same as the original study. Step 3: Define the dependent measure. Measure the 'bacterial colony count' after 24 hours. Step 4: Set sampling. Randomly assign bacteria to the four resulting groups (Media A + UV, Media A + Dark, Media B + UV, Media B + Dark) with at least n=6 samples per group.

common_mistakes: Changing multiple variables at once, which makes it impossible to isolate the cause of the result.
Reducing the sample size too low (e.g., n=2), which decreases the reliability of the data.
Changing the measurement timing or units from the original experiment, preventing a direct comparison.
Failing to include a control group that mirrors the original experimental conditions.
exam_tips: Look for the answer choice that changes ONLY the variable mentioned in the question prompt.
Ensure the sample size (n) is at least 6 or matches the original study's robustness.
Verify that the units of measurement (cm, grams, seconds) remain consistent with the original data set.
Eliminate choices that introduce 'new' equipment or methods not relevant to the specific factor being tested.
content.recap: To design a successful follow-up, isolate one independent variable with clear levels, keep all other original conditions as controls, define a specific measurement and time, and use random assignment with at least 6 samples per group.

knowledge_claims.content: The independent variable is the single factor deliberately changed between groups in a follow-up experiment.
A follow-up experiment should test only one new independent variable at a time to avoid confounding results.
Concrete levels must be defined for the independent variable, such as specific temperatures or concentrations.
Controls are the experimental conditions held identical to the original study to ensure differences trace back to the new factor.
The dependent measurement and the timing of that measurement must be explicitly defined in the follow-up design.
A valid follow-up experiment requires a minimum sample size of at least 6 samples per level (n ≥ 6) to detect changes reliably.
Random assignment or paired sampling should be used to assign subjects to experimental levels to avoid selection bias.
If only the chosen independent variable varies between identical groups, any consistent difference in outcome can be attributed to that variable.
It is a mistake to change both the independent variable and the measurement timing simultaneously in a follow-up design.
To verify a design, confirm that all original key conditions (like soil, light, or temperature) remain constant across all new test groups.
When testing if a new factor 'changes the effect' of an old factor, the experiment must include groups representing both factors.
A follow-up design is flawed if it fails to specify the units or method used to record the dependent variable.

items.stem:
SCIENCE PASSAGE 1: Leaf Gas Exchange Under Two Light Colors
Researchers placed two groups of equal-sized leaves from the same plant species in chambers. They exposed the leaves to blue light or red light at the intensities shown and measured net carbon dioxide uptake after 8 minutes. Positive uptake indicates that photosynthesis exceeded respiration.

Which statement correctly identifies variables in the study?

options.F: The measured outcome was held constant in every trial.
options.G: No condition was intentionally varied or classified.
options.H: Light color was one independent variable, and net carbon dioxide uptake was the dependent variable.
options.J: The graph title was the dependent variable.

items.explanation: The correct choice distinguishes the factor varied or classified from the outcome measured.

items.stem:
SCIENCE MATERIAL SET 2
Students tested how water temperature affected the time required for a tablet to dissolve. They used identical tablets, 101 mL of water in each cup, and stirred each cup at the same rate.

TABLE 1
Temperature (°C) | Dissolving time (s)
10 | 30
20 | 22
30 | 17
40 | 13

Trial 2 repeated the procedure with twice the water volume. Researcher 1 claims that higher temperature increases particle motion and therefore decreases dissolving time. Researcher 2 agrees that temperature matters but claims that stirring rate is the dominant factor whenever stirring is not controlled.

Which follow-up best tests Researcher 2's claim?

options.A: Vary temperature and stirring rate together.
options.B: Change tablet type without recording time.
options.C: Vary stirring rate while holding temperature constant.
options.D: Use one trial with no comparison condition.

videoLesson.title: Design a Single-Variable Follow-Up Experiment
videoLesson.description: You will identify the one independent variable, its concrete levels, and the dependent measurement to compare. Then state timing, random assignment, and ≥6 samples per level to isolate effects.
